title: Marburg Virus Disease (MVD): a rapid systematic review with narrative synthesis of epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostics, management, and public-health response

analysis.scope_and_question: Marburg virus (MARV) is responsible for a severe viral hemorrhagic fever characterized by high case-fatality rates and epidemic potential. Recent outbreaks from 2021 to 2025 across various African nations have brought renewed global focus.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We conducted a focused search across PubMed/PMC, WHO, CDC, NEJM, Lancet, Frontiers, and key public health sources up to 20 Nov 2025, using consistent search terms. Priority was given to primary outbreak reports, systematic reviews, and WHO guidance.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: MARV reservoirs are Egyptian fruit bats; human infections result from zoonotic spillover and subsequent human-to-human transmission, particularly via direct contact with bodily fluids and funeral practices. Case-fatality rates vary widely (roughly 24–88% historically), and average estimates are near 50% when aggregated across outbreaks. Clinical presentation ranges from abrupt febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms to coagulopathy, multi-organ failure, and hemorrhage. RT-PCR and antigen detection are the mainstays of early diagnosis; supportive care is the primary treatment. No licensed vaccine or antiviral existed as of November 2025, but several candidates and monoclonal antibody therapies are in development and clinical testing.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Marburg virus remains a high-consequence pathogen with substantial morbidity and mortality. We compiled evidence related to epidemiology, clinical features, diagnostics, management, prevention, and identified knowledge gaps.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Outbreak control relies on rapid surveillance, contact tracing, infection prevention and control (IPC) in healthcare settings, safe burial practices, and community engagement. Recent outbreaks have reinforced the need for rapid diagnostics, robust IPC in health facilities, accelerated clinical trials for therapeutics and vaccines, and improved ecological surveillance of bat populations and human exposures. Strengthening outbreak readiness and integrating MVD preparedness into routine public-health systems in at-risk countries should be a global priority.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on Marburg virus disease (MVD), covering epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostics, management, and public health response. MARV causes severe hemorrhagic fever with high case-fatality rates (24–88%, average ~50%), transmitted via zoonotic spillover from Egyptian fruit bats and human-to-human contact. Clinical features range from febrile illness to multi-organ failure and hemorrhage. Diagnosis relies on RT-PCR and antigen detection, with supportive care as the main treatment. No licensed vaccine or antiviral existed as of November 2025, though candidates are in development. Outbreak control emphasizes surveillance, IPC, safe burials, and community engagement. Key priorities include rapid diagnostics, robust IPC, accelerated therapeutic trials, ecological surveillance, and integrating MVD preparedness into public health systems in at-risk regions.

title: Digital Health for Pandemic Preparedness: A Critical Review of Innovations, Equity Gaps, and Governance in Infectious Disease Surveillance

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines digital health innovations for infectious disease surveillance, focusing on equity gaps and governance within pandemic preparedness. The central question concerns the role of digital health technologies in surveillance, detection, forecasting, contact tracing, governance, and equity.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a structured thematic narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature published from January 2010 to March 2025, following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from February 5 to 18, 2025, using keywords covering digital-health technologies, infectious diseases, and public-health functions. Records were deduplicated in EndNote X20 and screened by two blinded reviewers (Cohen κ = 0.81). Empirical studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, and reviews were appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Of 1498 records, 142 studies met inclusion criteria, with 48% rated as high quality. The evidence base is regionally skewed, with 41% from high-income countries and 19% from sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia. No technology was universally superior; AI studies were concentrated in high-income countries, while SMS mHealth studies were concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. Across the included studies, digital health is necessary but not sufficient for pandemic preparedness. Equity, sustainability, and accountability are constituents of effectiveness rather than obstacles.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The evidence base is heavily skewed regionally, with significant underrepresentation from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Recurring barriers include algorithmic bias, fragmented interoperability, donor-dependent sustainability, and slow benefit-sharing of pathogen data with LMICs. The binding constraint is increasingly political and institutional will rather than analytic uncertainty.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priorities should include addressing algorithmic bias, improving interoperability, ensuring donor-independent sustainability, and establishing equitable benefit-sharing mechanisms for pathogen data. Governance frameworks must be strengthened to ensure accountability and political commitment.

analysis.summary_en: This review assesses digital health innovations for infectious disease surveillance, focusing on equity gaps and governance in pandemic preparedness. A thematic narrative review of 142 studies from 2010 to 2025 found that digital health is necessary but not sufficient for preparedness, with no technology universally superior. The evidence base is regionally skewed, with 41% from high-income countries and 19% from sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia. Recurring barriers include algorithmic bias, fragmented interoperability, donor-dependent sustainability, and slow benefit-sharing of pathogen data with LMICs. The binding constraint is political and institutional will rather than analytic uncertainty. Implications include prioritizing equity, sustainability, and accountability in digital health implementation.

title: An operational One Health framework for enhanced multi-sectoral coordination and collaboration in Tanzania

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a context-specific One Health framework to enhance governance, communication, collaboration, and capacity building in Tanzania, addressing operational gaps identified through recent Marburg virus disease outbreaks.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross-sectional study included 101 participants from the health, livestock, agriculture, environment, and wildlife sectors across three regions (Arusha, Iringa, and Dodoma).
analysis.methods: Data were collected via semi-structured questionnaires and analyzed using quantitative and qualitative methods to assess knowledge, awareness, communication, and institutional structures.
analysis.main_results: Findings revealed weak inter-sectoral coordination, limited awareness of One Health guidelines, siloed operations, ad hoc communication, inadequate training, and insufficient financial resources, with only 33.7% of subnational participants aware of One Health and 27.7% able to identify its core elements.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of systemic fragmentation in One Health implementation, proposing a practical roadmap for institutionalizing the approach in Tanzania and similar contexts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The framework is expected to enhance preparedness, early detection, and response to health threats while fostering resilience and whole-of-government collaboration, providing a scalable model for strengthening health security.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is moderate due to the descriptive cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data, which may introduce recall bias and limit generalizability beyond the studied regions.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed an operational One Health framework for Tanzania by examining gaps in multi-sectoral coordination through a descriptive cross-sectional design involving 101 participants from health, livestock, agriculture, environment, and wildlife sectors. Key findings revealed weak inter-sectoral coordination, limited awareness of One Health guidelines (only 33.7% at subnational level), siloed operations, ad hoc communication, and insufficient resources. The proposed framework offers a practical roadmap for institutionalizing One Health, expected to enhance preparedness and response to health threats while providing a scalable model for similar contexts. Evidence strength is moderate due to the descriptive design and self-reported data limitations.
